ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Consultation — Christopher Reeve

code.originalText: Two-week review and physical medicine and rehabilitation (spinal cord injury medicine) consultation, with a bone density scan and kidney and bladder ultrasound

text.paragraph: Chronic incomplete C2 tetraplegia (ASIA grade C) in a 50-year-old director and advocate who uses a ventilator through a tracheostomy and had a diaphragm pacing system implanted some weeks ago. Please advise on pacer conditioning, review his autonomic dysreflexia plan, bladder and bowel management, bone health, spasticity and pain, and his seating and equipment. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: How should his diaphragm pacer time be stepped up, and what should stop a session?
Is the written autonomic dysreflexia plan, with nitroglycerin ointment as the medicine of choice, appropriate for him?
Is his bladder management with an indwelling catheter and yearly ultrasound appropriate, and how should kidney function be followed?
What do you advise for bone health, given his history of osteoporosis that reversed with his recovery program?
Does his spasticity or neck and shoulder pain need treatment beyond his exercise program?
What seating, pressure-relief and equipment review do you advise?

text.paragraph: Mr. Reeve, a 50-year-old director and advocate with a C2 spinal cord injury eight years ago, is seen at the request of Dr. Galloway. His physicians have published late recovery from ASIA grade A to C; he has sensation over much of his body and some voluntary finger and wrist movement, and continues stimulated cycling three times a week and weekly pool therapy. Some weeks after diaphragm pacer implantation he paces for two hours twice a day, tiring toward the end of each session, with saturation of 96 to 97%. His nurses suction a few times a day and use a cough-assist device each morning. He has an indwelling catheter and a daily morning bowel program, both working well. He has had no recent pounding headaches, flushing or sweating above the injury. His neck and shoulders ache after long days in his chair. His skin is intact. He wants to spend more time on the pacer and to keep working and traveling. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Christopher Reeve was born on September 25, 1952, in New York City. [D]
He was an actor who became a household name in the title role of the 1978 film Superman. [D]

On a Saturday at the end of May 1995, at 42, he was thrown headfirst when his horse stopped abruptly at the third obstacle of a cross-country event at an equestrian competition in Culpeper, Virginia. He was wearing a helmet. He broke his first and second cervical vertebrae, injured his spinal cord, and could not breathe on his own, as the University of Virginia neurosurgeon treating him reported. [D]

After months of therapy he was able to breathe for short periods without a respirator. He became an advocate for people with disabilities and for spinal cord research, lobbied Congress for better insurance protection against catastrophic injury, and directed the film In the Gloaming in 1997. [D]

The Christopher Reeve Paralysis Foundation, built on his advocacy and fundraising, became a leading source of money for spinal cord research, and he helped establish the Reeve-Irvine research center at the University of California, Irvine. [D]

He wrote about his life after the injury in an autobiography, Still Me, and in Nothing Is Impossible: Reflections on a New Life (Random House, 2002), which described his activity-based therapy and his return to work. [D]

His physicians at Washington University reported his case in 2002: his injury was classified as C-2, ASIA grade A, with no substantial recovery in the first five years. An activity-based recovery program begun in 1999 was followed over three years by improvement to ASIA grade C, with motor scores rising from 0 to 20 of 100, sensory scores from 5-7 to 58-77 of 112, and voluntary control of some muscles including the right half of the diaphragm. Reversal of osteoporosis, more muscle mass and less spasticity were associated with the recovery, medical complications fell, and infections and antibiotic use fell by more than 90 percent. [D]

In September 2002 the Associated Press reported that the first sign of change had been a movement of his left index finger almost two years earlier. He still used a wheelchair and a ventilator all but one hour a day and needed around-the-clock nursing care. He could feel about two-thirds of normal touch, which let him know when to shift his weight, so that he could sit in his wheelchair up to 16 hours a day without getting pressure sores. His program included electrically stimulated cycling for an hour three times a week and weekly pool therapy. Before it, his muscles had withered, his bones had thinned, and he had had repeated infections and life-threatening complications. [D]

In early 2003 surgeons at University Hospitals of Cleveland led by Dr. Raymond Onders implanted a diaphragm pacing system through small abdominal incisions. His phrenic nerves had not been injured. After eight years on a respirator, breathing through a tracheostomy, he could breathe for more than two hours without the respirator, and his doctors hoped the stimulation would let him wean further. [D]

list.item: Ventilator dependence with diaphragm pacing (Z99.11). Early conditioning is going well. The diaphragm needs gradual reconditioning; fatigue is the limiting factor. A backup ventilator and a power plan remain essential. [S]

Chronic incomplete C2 tetraplegia (G82.52). The autonomic dysreflexia plan is appropriate: remove the trigger first, and use a short-acting medicine only if systolic pressure stays at 150 mmHg or higher. Bone density is low at the hip and knee regions, without a fragility fracture; vitamin D is insufficient. Spasticity is mild and needs no medicine. The neck and shoulder aching is muscular, from head support and sitting time. His Braden score marks high pressure injury risk, and his seating has not been mapped since his recovery changed his posture and muscle bulk. [S]
Neurogenic bladder with an indwelling catheter (N31.9). Upper tracts normal on ultrasound; cystatin C is the right measure of kidney function at his muscle mass. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Galloway's intake note and the written autonomic dysreflexia plan. Intake results: cystatin C 0.92 mg/L with eGFR 90 (creatinine 0.48 mg/dL); calcium 9.0 mg/dL; PTH 52 pg/mL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL; albumin 3.8 g/dL; A1c 5.5%; LDL 104, HDL 34, triglycerides 170 mg/dL. DXA this morning: total hip T-score -1.6, with low distal femur and proximal tibia densities. Kidney and bladder ultrasound this morning: no hydronephrosis or stones; mild bladder wall thickening with the catheter in place. Braden 11. [S]

list.item: Step up each pacer session by about 15 minutes a week as tolerated, logged by his nurses; stop early for fatigue, breathlessness, or saturation below 94%; keep the ventilator ready at all times. [S]
Keep the written autonomic dysreflexia plan with nitroglycerin ointment as the as-needed medicine, train any new nurse before a first shift, and keep the wallet card in his chair bag. [S]
Continue the indwelling catheter with monthly changes; do not treat bacteria in the urine without symptoms; kidney and bladder ultrasound yearly; cystatin C every 6 to 12 months. [S]
Vitamin D3 2000 units daily with a recheck in about eight weeks; no bone-protective medicine now; continue stimulated cycling; careful transfers and ranging; repeat DXA in two years. [S]
No medicine for spasticity; daily ranging. For the neck and shoulder aching: head-support adjustment, heat and stretching, and acetaminophen as needed. [S]
Seating pressure mapping and cushion and head-support review with a seating clinic within a month. [S]
Keep the backup ventilator, suction, cough-assist device and generator checked monthly, and his power company and emergency services registration current. [S]
Spinal cord injury medicine review at least yearly, or sooner for any change. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Galloway, who sees him the same day. The plan was explained to Mr. Reeve and his nurse; he agreed and decides who else receives this note. [S]

Follow-up: Spinal cord injury medicine review in about one year, after the winter, or sooner for a pressure injury, repeated autonomic dysreflexia, or difficulty with the pacer; Dr. Galloway continues primary care and monitoring. [S]
